Does AI Reward High Skill Work? Evidence from US Labour Markets

Author

Riya Chandarana

Published

May 1, 2026

AI is reshaping the economy, the question on many peoples minds is whether they will benefit or lose out. The answer depends almost entirely on one thing. Not how much AI your job uses, but how much skill it requires. This blog uses data on 670 US occupations to show that AI exposure and high wages go together, but skill is the real driver. It reflects the fact that AI is most prevalent in occupations that were already highly skilled and highly paid long before AI arrived. This blog studies the relationship between occupation level AI exposure, pay, employment, and labour demand in the US. Combining an AI exposure index with labour market data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) and education information from the National Employment Matrix. These findings reflect associations rather than causal effects.

Research Questions

This blog answers the following question:

Are occupations with higher AI exposure better paid and does this relationship survive once occupational skill is taken into account?

Data

The analysis is a combination of five occupation level inputs:

  1. The AI occupation exposure index provides a measure of how exposed occupational tasks are to AI capabilities. Higher values indicate greater task exposure.

  2. BLS occupational employment and wage statistics provide employment levels and median annual pay by occupation.

  3. BLS employment projections provide average annual occupational openings, which I used as a measure for labour demand.

  4. BLS data on entry level education requirements are transformed into an ordinal scale, which serves as a measure of occupational skill.

  5. SOC occupation codes are used to align occupations across datasets, which ensures a consistent and accurate merge.

All BLS data and the AI exposure index reflects occupational conditions/AI capabilities in 2023. The AI exposure index, developed by Felten, Raj and Seamans (2023), measures the degree to which AI progress in specific capabilities such as language processing, reasoning, and image recognition overlaps with the tasks performed in each occupation.

The dataset contains 670 occupations. AI exposure is standardised with a mean near zero (negative values indicate a below average exposure and positive values indicate an above average exposure). Weekly pay and employment are highly skewed, which motivates the use of log transformations in the regression analysis. Skill level is measured on an ordinal scale from 0( no formal education required) to 6( doctoral degree required).

Figure 1: Average Weekly Pay Across AI Exposure Groups. Occupations are divided into quartiles based on their AI exposure level. Source: AI Occupation Exposure Index and BLS OEWS.

Figure 1 shows a clear stepwise increase in average pay across AI exposure groups, with high exposure occupations earning nearly double that of low exposure ones. This initially looks like strong evidence that AI rewards workers. However this pattern is misleading on its own, high AI exposure jobs also tend to require more education and skill. Due to this we are not able to tell whether it is AI or skill driving the wage difference.

Figure 2: AI Exposure and Log Weekly Pay by Occupation. Each point represents one occupation. The x-axis shows standardised AI exposure (higher values indicate greater exposure) and the y-axis shows log weekly pay in USD. Source: AI Occupation Exposure Index and BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics. Hovering over individual points allows you to see which occupations sit where.

Figure 2 confirms the raw positive relationship occupations with higher AI exposure scores tend to sit higher on the wage distribution. The upward sloping trend line suggests this is not driven by a handful of outliers but holds broadly across all 670 occupations. However, there is a considerable scatter around the trend line. Many low AI exposure occupations are well paid, and many high AI exposure ones are not. This variation hints that something else most likely skill is doing much of the explanatory work.

Regression Results

To test this more formally, I estimate occupation level regressions for wages. The baseline specification includes AI exposure only. I then added the skill measure, and finally an interaction between AI exposure and skill.

In the baseline model AI exposure is positively associated with pay. However, once skill is included the AI coefficient falls sharply, indicating that much of the baseline wage relationship reflects the fact that high AI occupations are also high skill occupations.

In the baseline model a one unit increase in AI exposure is associated with around 22% higher weekly pay which is a substantial difference. The baseline model explains around 30% of wage variation (R²=0.295). However, once skill is added this rises to 52% (R²=0.522). Showing that education level alone accounts for a large share of occupational pay differences. The AI exposure coefficient falls sharply from 0.217 to 0.029 and is no longer statistically significant (p=0.056). Meaning we cannot confidently say AI exposure itself is driving higher wages. Skill on the other hand remains strongly significant with a coefficient of 0.146. This tells us that the pay premium that appears to come with AI exposure is largely explained by the fact that AI exposed occupations tend to require higher levels of education and skill. In other words it isn’t AI exposure which makes a job well paid it is the skill required to do it.

AI exposure is positively associated with employment levels even after controlling for skill (coefficient = 0.473, p < 0.001). This suggests that AI exposed occupations are not shrinking they still employ large numbers of workers. For labour demand, once skill is controlled for, AI exposure shows no significant relationship with average annual job openings (p = 0.947), suggesting that while AI exposed occupations are large, demand for new workers in these roles is growing no faster than in occupations where AI plays a minimal role.

Robustness Checks

I use two robustness checks for the wage results:

First, I trimmed the top 5% of occupations by weekly pay, removing outliers such as surgeons and CEOs, to test whether the main findings are driven by a small number of extremely highly paid occupations.

Second, I estimated median regressions. These are less sensitive to skewness in the wage distribution and therefore provide a useful check on whether the baseline results are driven by the upper tail.

Both checks reinforce the main findings. The AI exposure coefficient remains small and statistically insignificant once skill is controlled for regardless of whether outliers are excluded or median regression is used.

The robustness checks broadly support the main findings. Trimming the top 5% of wages leaves the overall pattern intact, although the controlled AI coefficient remains slightly significant (p=0.021), which suggests a small association with pay. The median regression is more conclusive, once skill is controlled for the AI coefficient falls to just 0.007 and becomes statistically insignificant (p=0.718). Overall, the evidence consistently points to skill rather than AI exposure as the main driver of occupational pay.

Interpretation

The findings show that AI exposure is most concentrated in occupations already at the top of the skill and wage distribution. However the wage premium associated with AI exposure is largely explained by skill, as once education level is accounted for, AI exposure loses its explanatory power. This is consistent with Felten, Raj and Seamans (2023), whose AI exposure index shows that AI capabilities are seen most in occupations which require language, reasoning and analytical skills. It however does contrast with Frey and Osborne (2017), who estimate that nearly half of US jobs face significant automation risk, concentrated in routine and lower-skill roles. However exposure does not automatically translate into observable wage or employment effects at least not yet.

Limitations

This project has several limitations.

First, the analysis is cross sectional, meaning it captures a single snapshot in time rather than tracking changes over time and does not identify causal effects. The results should therefore be interpreted as associations.

Second, two workers in the same occupation may use AI very differently.

Third, the AI exposure measure captures task exposure rather than realised AI adoption. Exposure does not necessarily imply that employers have already adopted these tools.

Fourth, labour demand is measured using projected occupational openings rather than real time job postings. This is a reasonable measure, but it captures medium run demand rather than short run hiring dynamics.

These findings should be interpreted with caution. The data reflects occupational conditions in 2023, a period when AI adoption was still in its early stages. It is possible that the labour market effects of AI exposure will become more pronounced over time as adoption accelerates. The AI exposure scores themselves are also based on 2023 AI capabilities, which have since advanced considerably.

Machine Learning Evidence

To complement the regression analysis, I used a Random Forest model to predict log wages from occupation characteristics. Unlike standard regression, Random Forests can capture nonlinear relationships and interactions between features without requiring them to be specified in advance.

The cross validated R² ( a measure of how well the model predicts wages on unseen data) is just below zero meaning the model doesn’t reliably predict wages on data it hasn’t seen before. This is likely due to the small sample of only 670 occupations, as Random Forests usually require larger samples to generalise well. The feature importance scores remain interpretable despite the predictive accuracy. The real value of this approach is identifying which factors play the biggest role in determining occupational pay without relying on assumptions of standard regression.

Figure 3: Random Forest Feature Importance for Predicting Log Wages. Importance scores reflect the average reduction in impurity across all trees. Higher values indicate greater predictive contribution.

Figure 3 reinforces the regression findings. Education level dominates with an importance score of 0.722, followed by job advert intensity at 0.192. AI exposure ranks third at 0.048, which confirms that skill is the main driver of occupational pay. The low importance of the AI skill interaction term also suggests that the effect of AI exposure doesn’t vary significantly across skill groups.

AI Exposure and Job Outlook

If AI is really complementing workers, we would expect the most AI exposed occupations to also be the ones growing fastest more demand for AI capable workers should mean more hiring.

To test this, I collected job growth ratings for 342 occupations from the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, a government resource which predicts whether each occupation will grow, stagnate, or shrink over the next decade. Each occupation is rated as growing “Faster than average”, “Slower than average”, or showing “Little or no change”. These ratings were matched to the main dataset using a text similarity algorithm that links occupation names across sources even if they aren’t worded exactly the same. 174 of the 670 occupations in the sample were successfully matched.

Figure 4: Average AI exposure score by BLS job outlook category. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals. Source: BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook and AI Occupation Exposure Index.

Occupations projected to show “Little or no change” in employment have the highest average AI exposure score (1.15), while the fastest-growing occupations have the lowest (0.16). In other words, the jobs most exposed to AI are not the ones adding the most workers they are the ones standing still. This is the opposite of what a complementarity story would predict. It suggests that in heavily AI exposed roles, AI may be taking on tasks previously done by workers, reducing the need to hire more people rather than making existing workers more productive.

Conclusion

This project examines whether occupation level AI exposure is associated with wages, employment, and labour demand in the US.

The raw data shows a clear positive relationship between AI exposure and wages. But once occupational skill is controlled for, this wage effect disappears depending on specification. This indicates that the apparent AI wage premium largely reflects the fact that AI is concentrated in high skill occupations.

On the other hand, AI exposure remains positively associated with employment levels, suggesting that highly exposed occupations are not marginal or shrinking parts of the labour market.

From a policy perspective, these findings suggest that interventions aimed at improving wages in AI exposed occupations may be more effective if they are targeted at expanding access to education and skill development rather than AI adoption alone. If the wage premium associated with AI is primarily a skill premium, then policies focusing on up skilling workers may do more to reduce occupational inequality than those focused on AI diffusion specifically. This conclusion is also supported by the Random Forest analysis which identifies education level as the strongest predictor of occupational pay.

Overall, the results suggest that AI is concentrated in high skill, high paying occupations, but does not independently raise wage returns once skill is taken into account. The main implication is that AI may reinforce existing occupational inequalities not because it directly rewards exposure, but because it is most prevalent in occupations that are already skill intensive.

There is growing evidence that AI is beginning to reach into tasks once considered safely human. If that extends to lower skill occupations, the wage and employment patterns discussed above could look very different within a decade. The workers who currently sit outside the AI exposure distribution may find themselves inside it without the education levels that have so far meant high skill workers gain from AI rather than lose to it.

Replication Note

All data cleaning, merging, feature construction, regression analysis, and robustness checks are scripted in the src/ folder of the GitHub repository. The notebook uses the final processed dataset and saved regression outputs generated by that pipeline.

References

Felten, E., Raj, M., & Seamans, R. (2023). How will Language Modelers like ChatGPT Affect Occupations and Industries? Working paper, March 2023.

Frey, C. and Osborne, M. (2017) ‘The Future of Employment: How Susceptible Are Jobs to Computerisation?’, Technological Forecasting and Social Change, 114, pp. 254–280.

```{python}
import pandas as pd

summary['AI Exposure'] = summary['AI Exposure'].round(3)
summary['Weekly Pay (USD)'] = summary['Weekly Pay (USD)'].round(0).astype(int)
summary['Employment'] = summary['Employment'].round(0).astype(int)
summary['Skill Level'] = summary['Skill Level'].round(2)

summary.style.set_caption("Summary Statistics").format({
    'AI Exposure': '{:.3f}',
    'Weekly Pay (USD)': '{:,.0f}',
    'Employment': '{:,.0f}',
    'Skill Level': '{:.2f}'
}).format(subset=pd.IndexSlice['Count', :], formatter='{:.0f}')
```

# Regression Results
To test this more formally, I estimate occupation level regressions for wages. The baseline specification includes AI exposure only. I then added the skill measure, and finally an interaction between AI exposure and skill.

In the baseline model AI exposure is positively associated with pay. However, once skill is included the AI coefficient falls sharply, indicating that much of the baseline wage relationship reflects the fact that high AI occupations are also high skill occupations.

```{python}
wage_results = results[results["outcome"] == "log_pay"].copy()
employment_results = results[results["outcome"] == "log_employment"].copy()
demand_results = results[results["outcome"] == "advert_intensity"].copy()

key_models = ["baseline_full", "with_skill_full"]

wage_summary = wage_results[
    (wage_results["model"].isin(key_models)) &
    (wage_results["term"].isin(["ai_exposure", "skill"]))
][["model", "term", "coef", "p_value", "r_squared", "n"]].copy()

wage_summary["model"] = wage_summary["model"].replace({
    "baseline_full": "Baseline",
    "with_skill_full": "With Skill Controls"
})

wage_summary["coef"] = wage_summary["coef"].round(4)
wage_summary["p_value"] = wage_summary["p_value"].round(3)
wage_summary["r_squared"] = wage_summary["r_squared"].round(3)
wage_summary["n"] = wage_summary["n"].astype(int)

wage_summary.columns = ["Model", "Term", "Coefficient", "P-Value", "R²", "N"]

styled = wage_summary.style.format({
    "Coefficient": "{:.4f}",
    "P-Value": "{:.3f}",
    "R²": "{:.3f}",
    "N": "{:,}"
})
styled = styled.set_caption("Wage Regression Results (Full Sample)")
styled = styled.hide(axis="index")
styled
```

In the baseline model a one unit increase in AI exposure is associated with around 22% higher weekly pay which is a substantial difference. The baseline model explains around 30% of wage variation (R²=0.295). However, once skill is added this rises to 52% (R²=0.522). Showing that education level alone accounts for a large share of occupational pay differences. The AI exposure coefficient falls sharply from 0.217 to 0.029 and is no longer statistically significant (p=0.056). Meaning we cannot confidently say AI exposure itself is driving higher wages. Skill on the other hand remains strongly significant with a coefficient of 0.146. This tells us that the pay premium that appears to come with AI exposure is largely explained by the fact that AI exposed occupations tend to require higher levels of education and skill. In other words it isn’t AI exposure which makes a job well paid it is the skill required to do it.

AI exposure is positively associated with employment levels even after controlling for skill (coefficient = 0.473, p < 0.001). This suggests that AI exposed occupations are not shrinking they still employ large numbers of workers. For labour demand, once skill is controlled for, AI exposure shows no significant relationship with average annual job openings (p = 0.947), suggesting that while AI exposed occupations are large, demand for new workers in these roles is growing no faster than in occupations where AI plays a minimal role.


# Robustness Checks

I use two robustness checks for the wage results:

First, I trimmed the top 5% of occupations by weekly pay, removing outliers such as surgeons and CEOs, to test whether the main findings are driven by a small number of extremely highly paid occupations.

Second, I estimated median regressions. These are less sensitive to skewness in the wage distribution and therefore provide a useful check on whether the baseline results are driven by the upper tail.

Both checks reinforce the main findings. The AI exposure coefficient remains small and statistically insignificant once skill is controlled for regardless of whether outliers are excluded or median regression is used. 

```{python}
robust_compare = results[
    (results["outcome"] == "log_pay") &
    (results["term"] == "ai_exposure") &
    (results["model"].isin([
        "baseline_full", "with_skill_full",
        "baseline_trimmed", "with_skill_trimmed",
        "baseline_median", "with_skill_median"
    ]))
][["model", "coef", "p_value"]].copy()

robust_compare["model"] = robust_compare["model"].replace({
    "baseline_full": "Baseline",
    "with_skill_full": "With Skill Controls",
    "baseline_trimmed": "Baseline (Trimmed)",
    "with_skill_trimmed": "With Skill Controls (Trimmed)",
    "baseline_median": "Baseline (Median)",
    "with_skill_median": "With Skill Controls (Median)"
})

robust_compare["coef"] = robust_compare["coef"].round(4)
robust_compare["p_value"] = robust_compare["p_value"].round(3)
robust_compare.columns = ["Specification", "AI Exposure Coefficient", "P-Value"]
robust_compare.style.format({"AI Exposure Coefficient": "{:.4f}", "P-Value": "{:.3f}"}) \
    .set_caption("Robustness Checks — AI Exposure Coefficient on Log Wages") \
    .hide(axis="index")
```

The robustness checks broadly support the main findings. Trimming the top 5% of wages leaves the overall pattern intact, although the controlled AI coefficient remains slightly significant (p=0.021), which suggests a small association with pay. The median regression is more conclusive, once skill is controlled for the AI coefficient falls to just 0.007 and becomes statistically insignificant (p=0.718). Overall, the evidence consistently points to skill rather than AI exposure as the main driver of occupational pay.

# AI Exposure and Job Outlook

If AI is really complementing workers, we would expect the most AI exposed occupations to also be the ones growing fastest more demand for AI capable workers should mean more hiring.

To test this, I collected job growth ratings for 342 occupations from the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, a government resource which predicts whether each occupation will grow, stagnate, or shrink over the next decade. Each occupation is rated as growing "Faster than average", "Slower than average", or showing "Little or no change". These ratings were matched to the main dataset using a text similarity algorithm that links occupation names across sources even if they aren’t worded exactly the same. 174 of the 670 occupations in the sample were successfully matched.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

outlook_df = pd.read_csv("data/processed/final_analysis_data_with_outlook.csv")
outlook_df = outlook_df[outlook_df["bls_outlook"].isin(
    ["Faster than average", "Slower than average", "Little or no change"]
)]

group = outlook_df.groupby("bls_outlook")["ai_exposure"].agg(
    mean="mean",
    sem=lambda x: x.std() / np.sqrt(len(x))
).reset_index()

order = ["Faster than average", "Slower than average", "Little or no change"]
group["bls_outlook"] = pd.Categorical(group["bls_outlook"], categories=order, ordered=True)
group = group.sort_values("bls_outlook")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
bars = ax.bar(
    group["bls_outlook"],
    group["mean"],
    yerr=group["sem"] * 1.96,
    color="#4A9BAF",
    edgecolor="white",
    capsize=6,
    width=0.5,
    error_kw=dict(elinewidth=1.5, ecolor="#333333")
)

ax.bar_label(bars, fmt="%.2f", padding=6, fontsize=10)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.set_title("Figure 4: AI Exposure by BLS Job Outlook Category",
             fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xlabel("BLS Job Outlook Category", fontsize=11)
ax.set_ylabel("Average AI Exposure Score", fontsize=11)
ax.axhline(0, color="grey", linewidth=0.8, linestyle="--")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("output/figures/ai_exposure_by_outlook.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()
```

**Figure 4:** Average AI exposure score by BLS job outlook category. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals. Source: BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook and AI Occupation Exposure Index.

Occupations projected to show "Little or no change" in employment have the highest average AI exposure score (1.15), while the fastest-growing occupations have the lowest (0.16). In other words, the jobs most exposed to AI are not the ones adding the most workers they are the ones standing still. This is the opposite of what a complementarity story would predict. It suggests that in heavily AI exposed roles, AI may be taking on tasks previously done by workers, reducing the need to hire more people rather than making existing workers more productive.

# Conclusion

This project examines whether occupation level AI exposure is associated with wages, employment, and labour demand in the US.

The raw data shows a clear positive relationship between AI exposure and wages. But once occupational skill is controlled for, this wage effect disappears depending on specification. This indicates that the apparent AI wage premium largely reflects the fact that AI is concentrated in high skill occupations.

On the other hand, AI exposure remains positively associated with employment levels, suggesting that highly exposed occupations are not marginal or shrinking parts of the labour market. 

From a policy perspective, these findings suggest that interventions aimed at improving wages in AI exposed occupations may be more effective if they are targeted at expanding access to education and skill development rather than AI adoption alone. If the wage premium associated with AI is primarily a skill premium, then policies focusing on up skilling workers may do more to reduce occupational inequality than those focused on AI diffusion specifically. This conclusion is also supported by the Random Forest analysis which identifies education level as the strongest predictor of occupational pay. 

Overall, the results suggest that AI is concentrated in high skill, high paying occupations, but does not independently raise wage returns once skill is taken into account. The main implication is that AI may reinforce existing occupational inequalities not because it directly rewards exposure, but because it is most prevalent in occupations that are already skill intensive.

There is growing evidence that AI is beginning to reach into tasks once considered safely human. If that extends to lower skill occupations, the wage and employment patterns discussed above could look very different within a decade. The workers who currently sit outside the AI exposure distribution may find themselves inside it without the education levels that have so far meant high skill workers gain from AI rather than lose to it.
